opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, computational reproducibility is a really nice target for a few reasons. First, it's a task that sounds almost trivially simple but turns out to be surprisingly hard in practice. The idea is: you take a published paper, you take the code and data the authors released alongside it, and you try to rerun that code and get the same results that are reported in the paper. You're not trying to do new science, you're not even trying to replicate the experiment with new data. You just want to confirm that what's in the paper actually follows from what's in the repository.

And yet anyone who has tried this knows it's painful. Dependencies are missing or the versions have drifted, file paths are hard-coded to somebody's laptop, the README is out of date, there's some undocumented preprocessing step, the code takes three days to run on hardware you don't have. Studies across fields have found that a large fraction of papers with released code don't reproduce out of the box. So there's a real, unglamorous need here. Researchers, reviewers, journals would genuinely benefit from having this checked at scale, and right now basically nobody has the time to do it.

Second, from an AI evaluation perspective, it's a great benchmark because it's grounded in real-world messiness rather than toy puzzles. To succeed, an agent has to read documentation, figure out the environment, install things, debug errors, run long jobs, and then actually read the output and match it to a figure or table in the paper. That's a lot of the skill set we'd want from a capable research assistant or software agent. And crucially, there's a pretty clear notion of ground truth: either you got the reported number or you didn't. That makes it much easier to evaluate than open-ended tasks where judging success is itself subjective.

Third, and this is something I care about a lot, it's a way to test agents on something that's a prerequisite for the bigger claims people are making. You hear a lot of talk about AI that will automate scientific discovery. Well, before an agent can do novel science, it should probably be able to reproduce existing science, which is a much lower bar. When we built CORE-Bench, part of the point was to have a reality check. If agents struggle with this, that tells you something about how far we are from the more ambitious visions, and it does so in a concrete, measurable way rather than through hype or anecdotes.

And finally, it's a case where even partial success is useful. If an agent can reliably handle, say, half of the reproduction attempts and flag where it got stuck on the rest, that's already saving researchers a lot of time. So it's a nice combination: practically valuable, hard enough to be meaningful, and checkable enough to measure progress honestly.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility an unglamorous, practical task and contrasts it with automating scientific discovery, but does not distinguish it from reasoning challenges.

r002.rationale: It says partial success could save researchers time, but does not claim this would save tens of millions of hours per year.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that simple modifications to off-the-shelf agents substantially improve their accuracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reason I find computational reproducibility so compelling as a problem for agents is that it sits right at this sweet spot where it's genuinely hard, genuinely useful, and yet also tractable in a way that a lot of the more hyped agent tasks are not.

Let me say what I mean by that. If you take a published paper in machine learning, or economics, or really any computational field, and you try to reproduce the results starting from the code and data the authors released, that's often a miserable experience. Dependencies are missing, the random seeds aren't set, the paths are hard-coded to someone's laptop, there's a preprocessing step that's described in one sentence in the paper and isn't in the repository at all. We've found in our own lab that even when authors are acting in good faith and have released everything they think they need to, it can take a graduate student days or weeks to get a paper to actually run and produce the numbers in the tables.

So it's a real bottleneck for science. We talk a lot about the reproducibility crisis, and the computational part of that is in some sense the most fixable part, because in principle all the information is there. It's just an enormous amount of tedious, careful, somewhat adversarial debugging work. And that's exactly the profile of work that people hope agents can take on.

The second reason I like it is that it's a very honest benchmark for agent capability. A lot of agent evaluations we've looked at have problems. Sometimes the tasks are toy-like, sometimes the evaluation is contaminated because the solutions are on the web, sometimes it's unclear whether success actually means anything in the real world. Reproducing a paper doesn't have those problems. There's a ground truth, which is what the paper reports. The task is long-horizon, it requires reading documents, writing and running code, dealing with errors, and making judgment calls when the paper is ambiguous. And it's something a human expert would actually want done. So when we built CORE-Bench, part of the motivation was precisely to have an evaluation where if an agent does well, that tells us something meaningful, and where we could also be rigorous about cost, not just accuracy.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that reproducibility is a kind of safe harbor for agent deployment. If an agent fails at reproducing a paper, nothing bad happens. The harm is bounded. Compare that to agents doing things on your behalf on the open web, where mistakes can have consequences. So it's a domain where we can let agents operate with a fair amount of autonomy, learn what they're actually good and bad at, and build up trust in a way that transfers to higher-stakes settings later.

What we've found so far is sobering but encouraging. The best agents can handle the easier reproduction tasks reasonably well, but when you get to the hard versions, where they have to set up the environment from scratch and interpret the paper, performance drops off a lot. That gap is useful information. It tells us the limitation isn't really coding ability in the narrow sense. It's about sustained, careful execution over many steps, and knowing when you've actually succeeded versus when you've produced something that merely looks plausible. That's the same gap that shows up everywhere else people want to use agents, so I think making progress here will generalize.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility tedious and contrasts it with hyped agent tasks, but does not clearly distinguish it as a mundane task from aspirational challenges such as reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes reproducibility as a scientific bottleneck but does not state that solving it would save tens of millions of hours per year.

r003.rationale: It discusses agent performance generally but does not claim that simple modifications to off-the-shelf agents substantially improve accuracy.

astra-6.text:
Computational reproducibility gives us a fairly concrete way to ask whether an AI agent can do useful scientific work. You take a paper, its code, and its data, and ask: can you actually reproduce the reported results? The goal is clear, but the path can be quite messy. Dependencies may have changed, documentation may be incomplete, and there may be assumptions about how the data is processed that aren’t spelled out.

That makes it an interesting challenge for agents because it requires more than writing a piece of code. They have to investigate, run experiments, interpret failures, and decide what to try next. And they have to distinguish between getting something to run and actually reproducing the result.

There’s also a direct benefit to science. These are tasks that can consume a lot of researchers’ time. An agent that can reliably do even part of that work—or clearly explain where it got stuck and why—could make it easier for researchers to check and build on each other’s findings.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility a concrete challenge and contrasts it with merely writing code, but it does not distinguish it as mundane from aspirational AI challenges such as reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says agents could save researchers time, but gives no claim about immediately saving tens of millions of hours per year.

r003.rationale: It discusses what reproducibility requires from agents but does not state that simple modifications to off-the-shelf agents can substantially improve accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
Computational reproducibility is a nice test of whether an AI agent can do useful scientific work because the goal is concrete: take the code and data associated with a paper and try to reproduce its results. That sounds straightforward, but there’s often a lot of work between downloading a repository and getting the reported numbers. Dependencies may have changed, documentation may be incomplete, and there may be assumptions about the environment that were never written down.

So an agent has to do more than generate code. It has to investigate, run experiments, interpret errors, and decide what to try next. And it has to distinguish getting a program to run from actually reproducing the scientific result.

What makes this especially worthwhile is that the work has value beyond evaluating the agent. If agents can help researchers reproduce results—and clearly document where they succeed or get stuck—that could make it easier to check existing work and build on it.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility a concrete test and describes the work it involves, but does not distinguish it as mundane compared with aspirational AI challenges such as reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says reproducibility could help researchers check and build on work, but does not state that solving it would probably save tens of millions of hours per year.
